title: Artin join theorem for local integral algebras over henselizations
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $\mathfrak p_1,\mathfrak p_2\subset A$ prime ideals, and $D_i$ local commutative $A^h_{\mathfrak p_i}$-algebras integral over $A^h_{\mathfrak p_i}$, for $i=1,2$. Here $A^h_{\mathfrak p}$ means the henselization of $A_{\mathfrak p}$: the henselian local ring with its universal local map from $A_{\mathfrak p}$ (initial among local maps from $A_{\mathfrak p}$ to henselian local rings). For a ring $T$ and a connected component $Z$ of $\operatorname{Spec}T$, write $T_Z=T/I_Z$, where $I_Z$ is generated by the idempotents $e$ such that $Z\subseteq V(e)$; this is the component ring. Integral means that every element satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in the source ring. A ring is quasi-acyclic when all its component rings are henselian local [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Then $E=D_1\otimes_A D_2$ is quasi-acyclic. For any component ring $C$ of $E$, let $\mathfrak m_C$ be its unique maximal ideal. If both maps $D_i\to C$ are nonlocal, then $C/\mathfrak m_C$ is separably closed [def-kun-separably-closed]. If $D_i\to C$ is local for an index $i$, then this map is integral and $C/\mathfrak m_C$ is algebraic [def-weil-algebraic-element] over $D_i/\mathfrak m_{D_i}$. A homomorphism of local rings is local when the inverse image of the target maximal ideal is the source maximal ideal.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, printed p. 13; quasi-acyclic and component conventions, printed p. 12. Ordinary henselization convention also algebra.tex Tags 04GN (lemma-henselization) and 04GQ (definition-henselization).

proof.text: Use [lem-trf-henselizations-common-normal-cover] to choose a normal domain $P\twoheadrightarrow A$, primes $\mathfrak q_i$ over $\mathfrak p_i$, and local surjections $H_i=P^h_{\mathfrak q_i}\twoheadrightarrow A^h_{\mathfrak p_i}$. A quotient is integral: a class of $h$ satisfies $X-h=0$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive] makes each $D_i$ integral over $H_i$. Set $T=H_1\otimes_P H_2$. Because $P\to A$ is surjective and both actions on each $D_i$ factor through $A$, the $P$-balanced and $A$-balanced relations on $D_1\otimes_{\mathbf Z}D_2$ coincide: a coefficient $a\in A$ can be lifted to $p\in P$. Hence $E=D_1\otimes_A D_2=D_1\otimes_P D_2$, compatibly with its factor maps.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, quotient reduction to a normal domain; expanded using ordinary henselization quotients.

proof.text: Fix a component ring $U$ of $T$. By [lem-trf-normal-tensor-component-join-model], $U$ is a normal domain embedded in a separable closure of $\operatorname{Frac}(P)$ and is the subring generated by the two embedded $H_i$. The first assertion of [lem-trf-artin-embedded-hensel-join] makes this very ring $U$ henselian local. This applies to every component; it establishes quasi-acyclicity of $T$ before any residue alternative is used.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, normal-component embedding and application of Theorem 6.1.

proof.text: For any index $i$ with $H_i\to U$ local, the model lemma [lem-trf-normal-tensor-component-join-model] also gives that this map is ind-etale. Apply [lem-trf-ind-etale-local-henselian-integral] with source $H_i$, target $U$, and contracted prime $\mathfrak m_{H_i}$. Localizing $H_i$ at its maximal ideal changes nothing, and its henselization is $H_i$ itself: its identity map has the initial local-map property because it is already henselian. The conclusion is that $U$ is integral over $H_i$.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, local alternative; integrality obtained by the independently proved local ind-etale lemma.

proof.text: If both $H_i\to U$ are nonlocal, apply [lem-trf-nonlocal-join-internal-normalization] to the normal henselian embedded join $U$ supplied by Step 2. It gives a normal domain $P_0$ in a finite subfield of $\operatorname{Frac}(U)$ and two incomparable primes whose compatible henselizations generate exactly $U$. Regard the original ambient separable closure as a separable closure of $\operatorname{Frac}(P_0)$; this is valid because the intermediate field is finite separable over $\operatorname{Frac}(P)$. The incomparable-prime clause of [lem-trf-artin-embedded-hensel-join] now makes $U$ strictly henselian. Equality of the enlarged join with $U$ is essential here: no descent of separable closedness along a finite field extension is being assumed.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, normalization and incomparable-center argument; agent internal-normalization refinement before applying Theorem 6.1.

proof.text: The homomorphism $T\to E$ is integral. Indeed $T\to D_1\otimes_P H_2$ is the base change of $H_1\to D_1$, and $D_1\otimes_P H_2\to D_1\otimes_P D_2=E$ is the base change of $H_2\to D_2$. The base-change lemma [lem-weil-pbc-integral-base-change] gives integrality of both arrows; [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive] gives it for their composite. These identifications send a pure tensor to the same two factor images, so the composite is the original structural map.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, first proof sentence: integrality over the tensor product of the ordinary henselizations.

proof.text: Let $C=E/I_Z$ be any component ring. By the component convention in [lem-trf-affine-etale-cover-component-criterion], $\operatorname{Spec}C$ is precisely the nonempty connected space $Z$. Its image in $\operatorname{Spec}T$ lies in one connected component $W$. Write $U=T/I_W$. An idempotent defining $I_W$ maps to an idempotent of $C$ vanishing at every point of $\operatorname{Spec}C$; it is nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. Thus $T\to C$ factors through $U$. The monic equations of Step 5, reduced in $C$, show that $C$ is integral over $U$. Connectedness gives that $C$ has only the idempotents $0,1$. Since $U$ is henselian local by Step 2, [lem-trf-integral-component-henselian-permanence] makes $C$ henselian local, with $U\to C$ local and algebraic residue extension. This proves quasi-acyclicity of $E$. When $E=0$ there are no components and all its assertions are vacuous.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, integral-extension reduction; the component factorization is written explicitly.

proof.text: For this $C$ and $U$, locality of $D_i\to C$ is equivalent to locality of $H_i\to U$. First, $H_i\to D_i$ is local: its maximal ideal contracts to a maximal ideal by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-maximal-contracts-maximal], and $H_i$ is local. If $D_i\to C$ is local, its composite with $H_i\to D_i$ is local; as $U\to C$ is local, contraction then shows that $H_i\to U$ is local. Conversely, if $H_i\to U$ is local, the prime $\mathfrak r_i=(D_i\to C)^{-1}(\mathfrak m_C)$ lies over $\mathfrak m_{H_i}$. Since $D_i$ is integral over $H_i$, [lem-weil-pbc-integral-prime-over-maximal-maximal] makes $\mathfrak r_i$ maximal. It is therefore the unique maximal ideal of $D_i$, proving locality.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, integral-extension reduction; explicit transfer of the local/nonlocal alternatives.

proof.text: If $D_i\to C$ is local, Step 7 makes $H_i\to U$ local, so Step 3 gives that $U$ is integral over $H_i$. Step 6 gives that $C$ is integral over $U$, and [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive] makes $C$ integral over $H_i$. The same monic equations, with coefficients mapped along $H_i\to D_i$, prove integrality of $D_i\to C$. Reducing such an equation modulo $\mathfrak m_C$ shows that every element of $C/\mathfrak m_C$ is algebraic over $D_i/\mathfrak m_{D_i}$; locality ensures the latter is the canonically embedded coefficient field. This proves both parts of the local alternative for either index.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, case (2), including the residue-field consequence.

proof.text: If both $D_i\to C$ are nonlocal, Step 7 makes both $H_i\to U$ nonlocal, so Step 4 gives that $U$ is strictly henselian. Step 6 already supplies the integral $U$-algebra $C$ with no nontrivial idempotents. The strict clause of [lem-trf-integral-component-henselian-permanence] therefore makes $C$ strictly henselian. By [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], its residue field is separably closed, as required.

source.place: Theorem 6.3, case (1), and the integral-extension reduction.
